titleStmt.author: Viskontas
Quiroga
Fried

bibl.title: Human medial temporal lobe neurons respond preferentially to personally relevant images
bibl.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether single neurons in the human medial temporal lobe are more likely to respond selectively to images that are personally relevant to the patient
span.quote: Here, we address the question of whether individual neurons in the MTL show a preference for personally relevant pictures.

span.label: does personal relevance make a stimulus more likely to recruit a selective excitatory response from an MTL cell
span.quote: does a feature such as personal relevance, which may be related to the incidental recollection of autobiographically significant information ( 3 ), make a stimulus more likely to elicit a selective excitatory response from a cell?

span.label: grades selective MTL responsiveness by personal relevance — experimenters and family highest, celebrities intermediate, unknown faces lowest — and finds the gradient differs by MTL region
span.quote: Our findings indicate that personally relevant photographs are indeed more likely to elicit selective responses in MTL neurons than photographs of individuals with whom the patients have had no personal contact.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Our findings indicate that personally relevant photographs are indeed more likely to elicit selective responses in MTL neurons than photographs of individuals with whom the patients have had no personal contact.

span.label: personal relevance in human medial temporal lobe single-neuron responses
span.quote: Here, we address the question of whether individual neurons in the MTL show a preference for personally relevant pictures.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: To address this issue, we recorded the activity of 2,330 neurons in the human MTL while patients viewed photographs of varying personal relevance: previously unknown faces and landscapes, familiar but not necessarily personally relevant faces and landscapes, and finally, photographs of the patients themselves, their families, and the experimenters.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Personally relevant images are linked to more, and more varied, past experiences, so a larger number of MTL neurons are recruited to encode them
span.quote: Taken together, these findings suggest that personally relevant photographs are encoded by a larger number of neurons than photographs of unfamiliar people, because these photographs are associated with a larger number and perhaps wider variety of experiences.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Viewing a familiar face activates a richer network of associations than an unfamiliar one, and that richer network is what drives extra MTL cells into responding
span.quote: The images of experimenters and family members and, to a lesser degree, famous people, are all likely to elicit a richer network of associations than unknown faces, and thus recruit more MTL neurons.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Incidental (unintentional) recollection of the autobiographical network attached to an item is the route by which personal relevance enhances encoding
span.quote: One mechanism by which the self-referent effect might operate is via the incidental recollection of a rich network of information related to past experiences with that particular item.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: In the amygdala the driver is not personal relevance but a combination of novelty and emotional significance, which is why recently met experimenters outrank long-known family members there
span.quote: Notably, in the amygdala, photographs of the experimenters generated the largest proportion of responses, suggesting that these cells may represent other related variables, such as a combination of novelty and emotional significance.

span.label: the experimenters themselves are used as a stimulus category, which manufactures personal relevance the authors control rather than having to find it
span.quote: pictures of the researchers performing the experiments at the University of California at Los Angeles (UCLA), who had daily contact with the patients

span.label: relevance is turned into an ordered scale — unknown, famous, family, experimenter — so the prediction is a gradient rather than a single contrast
span.quote: Overall, we found that the different categories of faces (unknown, famous, family, and experimenters) generated different proportions of responses across the MTL [χ 2 (3) = 28.2, P < 0.001].

span.label: selectivity is defined by an exclusion rule rather than by a positive criterion: cells responding to more than five image sets are dropped so that promiscuous units cannot dominate the counts
span.quote: 12 units that responded to more than 5 pictures were excluded from the analysis, thus giving a total of 153 units with which we compared responses across the different category of stimuli.

span.label: responsiveness requires three conditions together — a five-SD threshold, a minimum absolute spike count, and a significance test — so no single loose criterion carries a unit through
span.quote: A unit was considered responsive if the activity to at least 1 stimulus fulfilled 3 criteria: ( i ) the median number of spikes was larger than the average baseline (for all repetitions of an image) plus 5 standard deviations; ( ii ) the median number of spikes was at least 2; and ( iii ) a t test comparing the baseline and response period for the particular stimulus showed a significant difference with P < 0.05.

span.label: the recency contrast is built into the stimulus set: experimenters are recent acquaintances and family remote ones, which turns the design into a test bearing on consolidation theory
span.quote: Given that experimenters are more recent acquaintances of the patients than their family members, this finding may be interpreted in light of the recent controversy regarding the extent to which recent and remote personal memories are represented in the hippocampus and surrounding cortices.

span.label: the counterargument to their own consolidation inference is written out by the authors rather than left to a critic
span.quote: Alternatively, proponents of MCT might argue that the specific memories contributing to the evocative power of images of family members and famous people in the hippocampus might be more recent in nature, or that the cells responding to images of remote acquaintances may be involved in reconsolidation or the formation of new memories involving viewing these images during the experimental protocol, or in the hospital setting.

span.label: duplicate views of the same person or landmark are dropped so that no category can win by being represented more often
span.quote: Duplicate images of the same individual or landmark shown in a different view were excluded. This procedure ensured that no category contained a disproportionate number of individuals in multiple views.

span.label: because image counts differ by patient and category, the metric is the proportion of images that elicited a response rather than the count
span.quote: The number of images in each category varied by patient and across categories, thereby leading us to use proportions of images eliciting responses in each category as the metric of interest.

span.label: a trivial face/non-face judgment is imposed purely to guarantee attention, not to measure anything
span.quote: This simple task, on which performance was virtually flawless, ensured that patients attended to the pictures.

span.label: the amygdala result is read against the grain of the paper's own thesis, as novelty and emotional salience rather than relevance
span.quote: Notably, in the amygdala, photographs of the experimenters generated the largest proportion of responses, suggesting that these cells may represent other related variables, such as a combination of novelty and emotional significance.

span.label: single units are separated from multiunits by four spike-train criteria including an explicit refractory-period check
span.quote: This was done based on ( i ) the spike shape and its variance, ( ii ) the ratio between the spike peak value and the noise level, ( iii ) the interspike interval (ISI) distribution of each cluster, and ( iv ) the presence of a refractory period for the single units (i.e., <1% spikes within less than 3 ms ISI).

span.label: Patients were never asked whether the images evoked episodic memories, so the recent-versus-remote memory question cannot be settled by the data.
span.quote: Because we did not ask our patients if the images we showed them generated episodic memories, we cannot address this issue directly with our current study.

span.label: Response counts per MTL region were low, so the regional differences must be read cautiously.
span.quote: Although the MTL regions showed different patterns of responsiveness to the different categories of photographs (see Fig. 3 ), the number of significant responses in each area was relatively low, and therefore these regional differences must be interpreted with caution, calling for further studies to elucidate the unique ways in which cells in these regions might code familiarity.

span.label: The null result for landmarks is inconclusive because no personally familiar landmarks were included in the stimulus set.
span.quote: Though we did not find any significant effects of familiarity with respect to landmarks, we did not include personally familiar landmarks such as the patient's home, school, or work.

span.label: the mechanism the whole account rests on — incidental recollection — was never measured
span.quote: Because we did not ask our patients if the images we showed them generated episodic memories, we cannot address this issue directly with our current study.

span.label: the faces-versus-landmarks asymmetry may be an artefact of the stimulus set, because no personally familiar landmarks were included
span.quote: Though we did not find any significant effects of familiarity with respect to landmarks, we did not include personally familiar landmarks such as the patient's home, school, or work.

span.label: the regional comparisons rest on small response counts and the authors say they must be read with caution
span.quote: the number of significant responses in each area was relatively low, and therefore these regional differences must be interpreted with caution, calling for further studies to elucidate the unique ways in which cells in these regions might code familiarity

span.label: images of the patients themselves produced almost nothing, so the self category had to be merged into family
span.quote: Of note, we found only 3 units that responded to images of the patients themselves. Therefore, we did not differentiate between pictures of the self and pictures of family members.

span.label: whether the famous-face responses in hippocampus involve personal recollection is left for future work
span.quote: Future studies should address the extent to which the specific photographs of family members and famous people that generated responses in the hippocampus were accompanied by incidental recollection of personal memories related to those individuals.

span.label: electrode placement was set by clinical criteria
span.quote: To obtain localizing information for potential curative resection, patients were stereotactically implanted with 6–14 depth electrodes from a lateral orthogonal approach aiming at targets selected using clinical criteria.

span.label: the self-reference effect, imported as the motivating prediction that personally relevant stimuli should recruit more neurons
span.quote: One virtually infallible method of enhancing memory is simply to relate the to-be-remembered information to one's self.

span.label: the sparse-coding expectation, carried across from animal MTL recordings and used to frame what a human selective response means
span.quote: In animals, selective sparse coding has also been observed in recordings from the MTL ( 15 , 16 ).

span.label: famous faces and names as a probe of semantic memory integrity, reused here as a graded familiarity stimulus set
span.quote: Furthermore, famous faces and names have long been used to query the integrity of recent and remote semantic memory in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) ( 3 , 6 – 11 ).

span.label: personal relevance — as connection to the self versus as accumulated shared experience; the paper opens on the first and its result rests on the second
span.quote: Taken together, these findings suggest that personally relevant photographs are encoded by a larger number of neurons than photographs of unfamiliar people, because these photographs are associated with a larger number and perhaps wider variety of experiences.

span.label: familiarity — as long-standing acquaintance (family) versus as recent daily contact (experimenters); the design treats both as personal relevance and finds them equal
span.quote: Family members and experimenters did not differ in their ability to elicit responses ( P = 0.47), but together, family members and experimenters were more likely to elicit responses than celebrities [χ 2 (1) = 13.1, P < 0.001], and celebrities were more likely to generate responses than unknown faces [χ 2 (1) = 4.5, P < 0.05].

span.label: familiarity versus recollection — in the models discussed, MTL cortex can support the first alone while the hippocampus is required for the second
span.quote: Several current theoretical models suggest that MTL cortex alone can support familiarity-based memory ( 17 , 33 ), whereas the hippocampus is necessary for the retrieval of episodic information, or recollection.

span.label: selective — as the cell's own tuning versus as an analysis threshold; here it is the latter, five image sets
span.quote: According to our criterion of selective responsiveness, which excluded neurons that responded significantly to more than 5 different sets of images (i.e., more than 5 celebrities, landmarks, or a combination), selective responses were seen in 153 units

span.label: MTL selectivity — as coding a person versus as coding the associations that person carries; the paper argues for the second
span.quote: The images of experimenters and family members and, to a lesser degree, famous people, are all likely to elicit a richer network of associations than unknown faces, and thus recruit more MTL neurons.

span.label: amygdala responsiveness — as personal relevance versus as novelty and emotional salience, which order the same stimuli differently
span.quote: Such an interpretation is supported by findings regarding the role of the amygdala in the processing of novel ( 41 , 42 ) and emotionally salient information ( 43 ), and the fact that unknown faces were just as likely as familiar faces to elicit responses in this region.

span.label: builds-on → Quian Quiroga, Reddy, Kreiman, Koch and Fried (2005), Nature 435(7045):1102-1107, on selective invariant MTL responses to famous people
span.quote: Recent findings from neurons in the human medial temporal lobe (MTL) have shown that individual cells respond selectively and invariantly to representations of famous people [Quian Quiroga R, Reddy L, Kreiman G, Koch C, Fried I (2005) Nature 435(7045):1102–1107].

span.label: extends → multiple trace theory (MTT) of medial temporal lobe memory function
span.quote: In line with MTT, the fact that both remote and recent acquaintances elicit cellular responses in the hippocampus and surrounding cortex seems to suggest that remote memories may be represented in the hippocampus proper, as well as in the surrounding regions.

span.label: extends → Quian Quiroga et al. 2005, that individual MTL neurons respond selectively and invariantly to famous people
span.quote: Recent findings from neurons in the human medial temporal lobe (MTL) have shown that individual cells respond selectively and invariantly to representations of famous people [Quian Quiroga R, Reddy L, Kreiman G, Koch C, Fried I (2005) Nature 435(7045):1102–1107].

span.label: builds-on → the self-reference effect literature on encoding enhancement
span.quote: The self-reference effect ( 1 ) is a well-documented encoding enhancement: people are more likely to remember items that are personally relevant, than items that have undergone some other deep or semantically elaborative encoding processes ( 2 ).

span.label: supports → multiple trace theory over the standard consolidation model, on the reading that recent and remote acquaintances alike drive hippocampal cells
span.quote: In line with MTT, the fact that both remote and recent acquaintances elicit cellular responses in the hippocampus and surrounding cortex seems to suggest that remote memories may be represented in the hippocampus proper, as well as in the surrounding regions.

span.label: supports → models in which MTL cortex supports familiarity while the hippocampus supports recollection
span.quote: A growing body of neuroimaging and neuropsychological studies now supports this idea ( 34 , 35 ).

span.label: builds-on → evidence that hippocampal cells code relative familiarity after a single presentation
span.quote: This hypothesis is in line with previous work showing that cells in the hippocampus code the relative familiarity of stimuli via alterations in firing patterns, even after only a single presentation of any given stimulus ( 37 , 38 ).

span.label: critiques → the state of the MTL regional division of labour, as unresolved despite extensive study
span.quote: The roles of the different regions of the MTL in declarative memory are still debated ( 32 ), despite the large number of studies designed to address this issue.

span.label: personal relevance —causes→ selective responsiveness
span.quote: Our findings indicate that personally relevant photographs are indeed more likely to elicit selective responses in MTL neurons than photographs of individuals with whom the patients have had no personal contact.

span.label: familiarity —distinct-from→ recollection
span.quote: Several current theoretical models suggest that MTL cortex alone can support familiarity-based memory ( 17 , 33 ), whereas the hippocampus is necessary for the retrieval of episodic information, or recollection.

span.label: multiple trace theory —contrasted-with→ standard model of consolidation
span.quote: Whereas the standard model of consolidation (MCT) predicts that over long periods of time, memories eventually become independent of the hippocampus ( 39 ), the idea that this structure is involved in episodic memory retrieval without regard to the age of the memory is one of the main tenets of an alternative theory of MTL memory function—namely, the multiple trace theory (MTT) ( 40 ).

span.label: hippocampus —part-of→ medial temporal lobe
span.quote: Sixteen patients participated in our study over 34 recording sessions, yielding a total of 2,330 units in 4 regions of the MTL: the amygdala, the hippocampus, the parahippocampal cortex, and the entorhinal cortex.

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · experimenters —contrasted-with→ famous faces
span.quote: Certainly, images of individuals with whom the patients are familiar, such as their family members or the experimenters, are more likely to generate richer autobiographical recollection than images of celebrities with whom they have had no personal interactions, or pictures of faces unknown to the patients.

span.label: sparse code —operationalised-as→ selective responsiveness
span.quote: Given that the MTL assigns a relatively small number of neurons to a specific stimulus ( 20 ), and that the number of stimuli in the environment is very large, does a feature such as personal relevance, which may be related to the incidental recollection of autobiographically significant information ( 3 ), make a stimulus more likely to elicit a selective excitatory response from a cell?

span.label: single units —distinct-from→ multiunits
span.quote: After sorting, the clusters were classified into single or multiunits.

span.label: amygdala —distinct-from→ personal relevance
span.quote: Notably, in the amygdala, photographs of the experimenters generated the largest proportion of responses, suggesting that these cells may represent other related variables, such as a combination of novelty and emotional significance.

span.label: landmarks —contrasted-with→ famous faces
span.quote: In contrast to cellular responses to faces, which showed a significant preference for famous faces, as compared with unknown faces [χ 2 (1) = 4.5, P < 0.05], there was no difference in the proportion of cells responding to famous versus unknown landmarks ( P = 0.27), as 14% of the famous landmarks generated responses, whereas 11% of the unknown landmarks did the same.

span.label: autobiographical memory —causes→ medial temporal lobe
span.quote: Finally, autobiographical memory retrieval consistently engages the medial temporal lobe ( 12 ), suggesting that cells in this region may respond differentially to faces that elicit autobiographical memory retrieval.

span.label: personal relevance —causes→ incidental recollection
span.quote: For example, a picture of a patient's mother shown during the experiment may automatically generate retrieval of a personal memory, such as her recent visit to the hospital, or an incident on a family vacation that occurred many years ago.

span.label: experimenters —contrasted-with→ famous faces
span.quote: And, as in the entorhinal cortex, categories of family members and experimenters did not differ ( P > 0.5), though together they were more likely to elicit responses than famous faces: [χ 2 (1) = 42.3, P < 0.01].

span.label: chi-squared test
span.quote: we ran a χ 2 test including responses collapsed across all of the regions, a second χ 2 test (number of response-generating images per region) to check if there was a difference between regions in terms of the pattern of responses, and finally, a separate χ 2 test to investigate differences in category response patterns for each MTL subregion separately.

span.label: t-test
span.quote: A unit was considered responsive if the activity to at least 1 stimulus fulfilled 3 criteria: ( i ) the median number of spikes was larger than the average baseline (for all repetitions of an image) plus 5 standard deviations; ( ii ) the median number of spikes was at least 2; and ( iii ) a t test comparing the baseline and response period for the particular stimulus showed a significant difference with P < 0.05.

span.label: median
span.quote: The response to a picture was defined as the median number of spikes across trials in the first second after stimulus onset.

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: A unit was considered responsive if the activity to at least 1 stimulus fulfilled 3 criteria: ( i ) the median number of spikes was larger than the average baseline (for all repetitions of an image) plus 5 standard deviations; ( ii ) the median number of spikes was at least 2; and ( iii ) a t test comparing the baseline and response period for the particular stimulus showed a significant difference with P < 0.05.

span.label: planned comparisons
span.quote: we then conducted the following 3 planned comparisons: images of family members vs. experimenters, images of family members and experimenters vs. celebrities, and images of celebrities vs. unknown faces.

span.label: post-hoc tests
span.quote: there was a regional difference in terms of responsiveness [χ 2 (3) = 8.4, P < 0.05], and post-hoc tests demonstrated that the entorhinal cortex showed fewer responses than the hippocampus [χ 2 (1) = 6.0, P < 0.01] and parahippocampal cortex [χ 2 (1) = 5.4, P < 0.05].

span.label: p-value
span.quote: In the hippocampus there was a significant difference among these categories [χ 2 (3) = 9.2, P < 0.05].

span.label: χ 2
span.quote: the different categories of faces (unknown, famous, family, and experimenters) generated different proportions of responses across the MTL [χ 2 (3) = 28.2, P < 0.001]

span.label: planned comparisons
span.quote: To further evaluate the differences in responses in terms of personal relevance, we conducted the following 3 planned comparisons: images of family members vs. images of experimenters, images of family members and experimenters vs. celebrities, and images of celebrities vs. unknown faces.

span.label: post-hoc tests
span.quote: post-hoc tests demonstrated that the entorhinal cortex showed fewer responses than the hippocampus [χ 2 (1) = 6.0, P < 0.01]

span.label: t test
span.quote: a t test comparing the baseline and response period for the particular stimulus showed a significant difference with P < 0.05

span.label: median number of spikes
span.quote: The response to a picture was defined as the median number of spikes across trials in the first second after stimulus onset.

span.label: 4(region) × 4(category) χ 2 analysis
span.quote: we ran a 4(region) × 4(category) χ 2 analysis and found that the regions did in fact show significantly different patterns: [χ 2 (9) = 32.3, P < 0.0001]

span.label: Photographs of the experimenters elicited selective responses from 22% of the image-cell pairs and photographs of the patients' own families 17%, versus 9% for famous faces and 5% for unknown faces.
span.quote: Photographs of the experimenters were most likely to generate a response (22%), followed by photographs of the patients and their families (17%).

span.label: Family members and experimenters were statistically indistinguishable from each other but together beat celebrities, and celebrities in turn beat unknown faces, giving a graded ladder of personal relevance.
span.quote: Family members and experimenters did not differ in their ability to elicit responses ( P = 0.47), but together, family members and experimenters were more likely to elicit responses than celebrities [χ 2 (1) = 13.1, P < 0.001], and celebrities were more likely to generate responses than unknown faces [χ 2 (1) = 4.5, P < 0.05].

span.label: Familiarity produced no such effect for places: famous landmarks (14%) and unknown landmarks (11%) elicited statistically indistinguishable proportions of responses.
span.quote: there was no difference in the proportion of cells responding to famous versus unknown landmarks ( P = 0.27), as 14% of the famous landmarks generated responses, whereas 11% of the unknown landmarks did the same.

span.label: Selective excitatory responses were not spread evenly over the MTL: entorhinal cortex yielded fewer responses than either the hippocampus or the parahippocampal cortex.
span.quote: there was a regional difference in terms of responsiveness [χ 2 (3) = 8.4, P < 0.05], and post-hoc tests demonstrated that the entorhinal cortex showed fewer responses than the hippocampus [χ 2 (1) = 6.0, P < 0.01] and parahippocampal cortex [χ 2 (1) = 5.4, P < 0.05].

span.label: The four MTL regions differed significantly from one another in how they distributed responses across the four face categories.
span.quote: To investigate whether the different MTL regions showed different patterns of responses, we ran a 4(region) × 4(category) χ 2 analysis and found that the regions did in fact show significantly different patterns: [χ 2 (9) = 32.3, P < 0.0001].

span.label: The hippocampus was the one region where celebrities behaved like personally known people, responding more to famous than to unknown faces while family, experimenters and celebrities did not differ from each other.
span.quote: whereas categories of family members, experimenters, and celebrities showed no significant differences ( P > 0.5), celebrities were more likely to generate responses than unknown faces: [χ 2 (1) = 10.9, P < 0.01].

span.label: In entorhinal cortex no unit at all responded to unknown faces.
span.quote: In entorhinal cortex, we did not find any responses to unknown faces.

span.label: In the amygdala the ordering reversed at the top end: experimenters elicited responses more often than family members.
span.quote: with experimenters showing a greater propensity for response elicitation than family members [χ 2 (1) = 3.94, P < 0.05]

span.label: Images of the patients themselves were an exception with only 3 responsive units, too few to treat self-images separately from family images.
span.quote: Of note, we found only 3 units that responded to images of the patients themselves.

span.label: Overall, personally relevant photographs are more likely to elicit selective MTL responses than photographs of people the patient has never met.
span.quote: Our findings indicate that personally relevant photographs are indeed more likely to elicit selective responses in MTL neurons than photographs of individuals with whom the patients have had no personal contact.

span.label: response likelihood was ordered by personal relevance: experimenters 22%, family 17%, celebrities 9%, unknown faces 5%
span.quote: Photographs of the experimenters were most likely to generate a response (22%), followed by photographs of the patients and their families (17%). Pictures of famous faces, in turn, yielded fewer responses (9%), and the unknown faces generated the fewest responses (5%).

span.label: family and experimenters were indistinguishable, but together beat celebrities, which in turn beat unknown faces
span.quote: Family members and experimenters did not differ in their ability to elicit responses ( P = 0.47), but together, family members and experimenters were more likely to elicit responses than celebrities [χ 2 (1) = 13.1, P < 0.001], and celebrities were more likely to generate responses than unknown faces [χ 2 (1) = 4.5, P < 0.05].

span.label: the familiarity effect held for faces but not for landmarks — 14% famous against 11% unknown
span.quote: there was no difference in the proportion of cells responding to famous versus unknown landmarks ( P = 0.27), as 14% of the famous landmarks generated responses, whereas 11% of the unknown landmarks did the same

span.label: only 3 units responded to images of the patients themselves, so self and family were merged
span.quote: Of note, we found only 3 units that responded to images of the patients themselves. Therefore, we did not differentiate between pictures of the self and pictures of family members.

span.label: the four MTL regions differed in their category response patterns
span.quote: To investigate whether the different MTL regions showed different patterns of responses, we ran a 4(region) × 4(category) χ 2 analysis and found that the regions did in fact show significantly different patterns: [χ 2 (9) = 32.3, P < 0.0001].

span.label: the hippocampus was the only region where famous faces beat unknown faces, with family, experimenters and celebrities not differing from each other
span.quote: Furthermore, whereas categories of family members, experimenters, and celebrities showed no significant differences ( P > 0.5), celebrities were more likely to generate responses than unknown faces: [χ 2 (1) = 10.9, P < 0.01].

span.label: entorhinal cortex produced no responses at all to unknown faces
span.quote: In entorhinal cortex, we did not find any responses to unknown faces.

span.label: in parahippocampal cortex family and experimenters together beat famous faces strongly, and famous did not beat unknown
span.quote: And, as in the entorhinal cortex, categories of family members and experimenters did not differ ( P > 0.5), though together they were more likely to elicit responses than famous faces: [χ 2 (1) = 42.3, P < 0.01]. Famous faces did not differ from unknown faces with respect to their ability to generate responses ( P > 0.1).

span.label: in the amygdala experimenters beat family, and neither the celebrity nor the unknown contrast held — the familiarity ordering broke down
span.quote: with experimenters showing a greater propensity for response elicitation than family members [χ 2 (1) = 3.94, P < 0.05], but no difference between family and experimenters together vs. celebrities ( P > 0.4) and no difference between celebrities and unknown faces ( P > 0.2)

span.label: selective responses were unevenly distributed across MTL, with entorhinal cortex responding less than hippocampus and parahippocampal cortex
span.quote: there was a regional difference in terms of responsiveness [χ 2 (3) = 8.4, P < 0.05], and post-hoc tests demonstrated that the entorhinal cortex showed fewer responses than the hippocampus [χ 2 (1) = 6.0, P < 0.01] and parahippocampal cortex [χ 2 (1) = 5.4, P < 0.05]

span.label: an amygdala unit responded to one researcher's photograph and to none of 100+ perceptually similar images
span.quote: This neuron responded only to a picture of one of the researchers performing experiments at UCLA and not to 100+ other stimuli that were perceptually similar.

span.label: the selectivity exclusion removed only 7% of responsive units
span.quote: This procedure resulted in the exclusion of only 7% of all of the responsive units (165 in total).

span.label: self-reference effect
span.quote: The self-reference effect ( 1 ) is a well-documented encoding enhancement: people are more likely to remember items that are personally relevant, than items that have undergone some other deep or semantically elaborative encoding processes ( 2 ).

span.label: criterion of selective responsiveness
span.quote: According to our criterion of selective responsiveness, which excluded neurons that responded significantly to more than 5 different sets of images (i.e., more than 5 celebrities, landmarks, or a combination), selective responses were seen in 153 units

span.label: response to a picture
span.quote: The response to a picture was defined as the median number of spikes across trials in the first second after stimulus onset.

span.label: responsive unit
span.quote: A unit was considered responsive if the activity to at least 1 stimulus fulfilled 3 criteria: ( i ) the median number of spikes was larger than the average baseline (for all repetitions of an image) plus 5 standard deviations; ( ii ) the median number of spikes was at least 2; and ( iii ) a t test comparing the baseline and response period for the particular stimulus showed a significant difference with P < 0.05.

span.label: multiple trace theory (MTT)
span.quote: the idea that this structure is involved in episodic memory retrieval without regard to the age of the memory is one of the main tenets of an alternative theory of MTL memory function—namely, the multiple trace theory (MTT) ( 40 )

span.label: sparse code in the MTL
span.quote: In fact, the idea that the MTL represents information using a sparse code is one of the basic tenets of most contemporary memory models

span.label: The self-reference effect
span.quote: The self-reference effect ( 1 ) is a well-documented encoding enhancement: people are more likely to remember items that are personally relevant, than items that have undergone some other deep or semantically elaborative encoding processes ( 2 ).

span.label: selective responsiveness
span.quote: our criterion of selective responsiveness, which excluded neurons that responded significantly to more than 5 different sets of images (i.e., more than 5 celebrities, landmarks, or a combination)

span.label: response
span.quote: The response to a picture was defined as the median number of spikes across trials in the first second after stimulus onset.

span.label: baseline
span.quote: Similarly, the baseline for each picture was the median number of spikes in the second before stimulus onset.

span.label: multiple trace theory
span.quote: the idea that this structure is involved in episodic memory retrieval without regard to the age of the memory is one of the main tenets of an alternative theory of MTL memory function—namely, the multiple trace theory (MTT) ( 40 )

span.label: standard model of consolidation
span.quote: the standard model of consolidation (MCT) predicts that over long periods of time, memories eventually become independent of the hippocampus ( 39 )

span.label: personal relevance category of the presented image (self/family, experimenters, celebrities, unknown faces, famous and unknown landmarks)
span.term: personal relevance category of the presented image (self/family, experimenters, celebrities, unknown faces, famous and unknown landmarks)
span.quote: We showed the patients 6 categories of images: photographs of the patient and his/her family and friends, photographs of the experimenters, photographs of famous celebrities, photographs of unknown faces, photographs of famous landmarks such as the Taj Mahal, and finally photographs of unknown landmarks, such as a Victorian house or an unknown building.

span.label: proportion of images in a category that elicited a selective response
span.term: proportion of images in a category that elicited a selective response
